title: Connection Pooling
subtitle: Managing database connections at scale with PgBouncer, ProxySQL, and transaction-level multiplexing.
keyTakeaways: Allocating too many database connections degrades throughput: CPU cores waste cycles on context-switching and lock contention rather than executing queries.
In PostgreSQL, each connection is an independent operating system process consuming 5-10 MB of memory; 1,000 idle connections waste ~10 GB of database RAM.
Transaction-level pooling via PgBouncer allows thousands of client applications to share a small pool of database connections, checking out a connection only while a transaction runs.
architectureDiagram:
TRANSACTION-LEVEL CONNECTION POOLING (PGBOUNCER)
[ 2,000 Application Client Connections ]
                 |
                 v (Client connections held idle between queries)
      [ PgBouncer Connection Proxy ]
                 |
                 v (Only 40 Active Physical Server Connections!)
      [ PostgreSQL Database Server ]
      (Zero process bloat; CPU cores execute queries at 100% efficiency)

sections.heading: Why Excessive Connections Degrade Performance
sections.body: A common operational mistake during traffic surges is increasing `max_connections` from 200 to 2,000. In PostgreSQL, each client connection spawns a dedicated OS process. Having 2,000 concurrent processes on a 16-core machine causes extreme kernel scheduling overhead, CPU cache thrashing, and memory exhaustion. The database spends more time context-switching between connections than executing SQL.
bullets: Process Memory Footprint: 2,000 connections allocate 10-20 GB of RAM solely for process state and connection buffers.
Lock Table Contention: Concurrent transactions share global memory structures for locking and snapshot visibility; higher connection counts inflate lock acquisition latency.
The Optimal Connection Sweet Spot: PostgreSQL performance peaks when active connection count is constrained to approximately `(2 * CPU cores) + disk channels`.

codeSnippet.title: PgBouncer Configuration for Transaction Pooling (pgbouncer.ini)
codeSnippet.code:
[databases]
production_db = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=production_db

[pgbouncer]
listen_port = 6432
listen_addr = *
auth_type = scram-sha-256
# Transaction mode: connection returned to pool immediately on COMMIT/ROLLBACK
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000
default_pool_size = 40
reserve_pool_size = 10

sections.heading: Session vs Transaction vs Statement Pooling
sections.body: External connection proxies (PgBouncer for Postgres, ProxySQL for MySQL) operate under three distinct pooling modes.
bullets: Session Pooling: The client claims a physical database connection upon connect and holds it until disconnect. Provides basic connection reuse, but offers minimal multiplexing benefit during traffic spikes.

Transaction Pooling: The client claims a physical connection only for the duration of a transaction (`BEGIN ... COMMIT`). Between transactions, the client stays connected to PgBouncer while the underlying database connection serves other clients. Trade-off: session-level features (prepared statements, advisory locks, `SET search_path`) cannot be used safely.
Statement Pooling: The connection returns to the pool after each individual statement. Does not support multi-statement transactions.

tradeOffs.pros: Allows 10,000+ client connections to share 50 database connections; shields database from serverless scaling spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Breaks session-level SQL features (temporary tables, named prepared statements without pgbouncer 1.21+ workarounds).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Serverless AWS Lambda architectures, microservice fleets, and high-concurrency web applications.

tradeOffs.pros: Full support for all session features, prepared statements, and advanced ORM capabilities; zero extra proxy hops.
tradeOffs.cons: Connection count scales linearly with application pod count; scaling up containers risks crashing the database.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Monolithic applications with fixed, predictable instance counts.

interviewTip: When designing high-scale architectures with serverless functions (like AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Functions), always include an external connection pooler: 'Because serverless containers scale to thousands of instances in seconds, direct connections would crash the database. We will place PgBouncer or AWS RDS Proxy in front of the database to multiplex thousands of client connections into 50 physical connections.'
